newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Africa seen having bright future in zinc.
newsitem.headline: Africa seen having bright future in zinc.

text.p: Africa, currently a bit player in world terms for the production and consumption of refined zinc and zinc products, has a potentially pivotal role to play in coming years, a conference on the metal was told on Tuesday.

"Africa must be regarded as an emerging market for the 21st century, with significant potential for growth in zinc production and consumption," Hugh Callaghan, Marketing Manager of the Zinc Corporation of South Africa Limited, told the second day of the three-day "Zinc and its markets conference" organised by Metal Bulletin magazine.

"There is, we believe, considerable cause for optimism in that the broad-based political movement which has emerged in the Great Lakes region of Africa has a political and economic vision close to that of President Museveni of Uganda," Callaghan said.
"Once this movement comes to power, a combination of progressive economic management and democratic government will be underpinned by massive foreign aid and World Bank intervention," he added.
Callaghan said Africa would account for two percent of world zinc production, consumption and smelting capacity in 1997 and would remain marginal even if everything developed well.
Its short-term significance lay more in its ability to make good any shortfalls in the metals or concentrates markets, Callaghan told the conference.
He said Kipushi mine in Zaire's rebel-held Shaba province had great potential, with high grade reserves valued at $6.2 billion and a further 25 million tonnes of zinc contained in mine tailings.
Callaghan said there had been reports that creation of a smelter with an annual capacity of 200,000 tones of zinc is under consideration.
The Broken Hill, Maranda and Rosh Pinah mines in South Africa and Namibia had combined output of zinc metal in concentrates of over 100,000 tonnes, he said.
Rosh Pinah in particular had reserves estimated at 13.5 million tonnes grading at 6.5 percent.

Callaghan said South Africa and Zaire represented the most likely sources of growth in refined zinc production, whereas West Africa and Southern Africa were the most likely growth areas for consumption of the refined metal.
The problems, he said, were primarily economic, political and logistical.
However, one factor that could not be ignored was the relatively more relaxed approach in Africa than in Europe to environmental problems.
This would tend to influence the future decisions of smelter operators -- in some parts of Europe facing major clean-up bills -- on where to set up operations, Callaghan said.

"While this paper in no way suggests that a cavalier approach to such matters exists in Africa, or should exist for that matter, restrictive environmental practices are going to play an increasing role in decisions on the siting of smelters in the future," he added.
